utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, David O'Brien, and David Martini appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before the witness comes in, I just have one query. We hope today or tomorrow to be able to provide Your Honours with the cleaned up, if that's the right expression, 65 ter list. What we simply want to know is this: We proposed simply to send it to all parties via e-mail, unless Your Honours think that we need to file it as a separate motion. But, otherwise, we're simply -- it -- it's the cleaned up -- with hopefully all duplicates removed and the like. So we're in Your Honours' hands on this. We thought you probably didn't want another motion; but if you do, we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We agree that the -- it -- we understand why you would wish to avoid the formalities, to avoid a formal filing. But inasmuch as it is a formal document, we see no way around that. So it would be -- it's -- so -- so that's the way it would have to be. I don't expect that -- I suppose it would be an addendum to your earlier filing. But it should be in that form in our view.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it will simply be -- it'll be filed as revised 65 ter, Your Honours, I would have thought. My only hesitation in saying it is -- when I say "cleaned up," I mean, something always manages to escape even six people's eagle eye. And so I didn't want them to do yet another filing, if possible, to say, Sorry, we've got to correct that because we've discovered yet another duplicate. But if Your Honours think, as it's a formal document, it should be filed, then we will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. While the blinds are being raised, I remind you, before counsel resumes her examination-in-chief, you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, we left off yesterday looking at the report in respect of the events of 1992. And I want you to look at one other description on the same lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up on the screen, please, the document which is at tab 50, which is 39 -- 65 ter 395.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is dated - the number isn't on it - the 8th of February, 1993, and it's called a record.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we go, please, to the third page in English and the second page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who signed -- who signed that report [Microphone not activated] ... or whose signature appears there?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now? Are you getting translation? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We have the translation, so probably there is a -- some problem with the -- with the connection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you hear us now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, do you recognise the signature there?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The station commander, Jovan Skobo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The man you were telling us about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's go back, please, then, to the beginning of the report, first page -- or record. This is -- it starts by saying: "This is done on the 8th of February, 1993, at the premises of Pale SJB in connection with the handover of the police station from the former chief Malko Koroman to the new SJB chief Petko Pekic." And then it goes on to give some explanation. Was it standard that when there was a change in the head of an SJB, there would be, as it were, a briefing from someone at the station on the events that had taken place?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then, if we look at what was said -- or some of what was said: "Due to the security reasons, in mid-March the police station disarmed the non-Serb police employees and removed them from service; weapons owned by non-Serb citizens were seized, irrespective of whether they had permits for them or not ..." And does that, sir, accord with what you told us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such situations, during the handover of the station from one commander to another, usually a commission is set up in the main office, in the MUP. And that commission attends such a handover. And this record shows only the signature of Jovan Skobo, so I don't know whether this was a internal affair, an internal takeover, or was it an official affair, just as it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 4, 15, the witness says either main office in the MUP or -- and this wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, could you repeat what you said where this handover -- where the commission is. "It's set up in the main office in the MUP or ..." Where else could it have been?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During a handover from one commander to another at a police station and especially in the case of the chief of that police station, then either the minister or one of his associates, either a deputy or an assistant, sets up a commission which includes representatives -- a representative of the MUP and a representative of the public security centre who attend the handover to make sure that everything is done according to the law. In this particular case, I don't know whether that was, indeed, the case because the only signature on the document is by Jovan Skobo, as the station commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. All I was actually asking, sir, was whether those few -- first few lines sum up what you told us had been happening in 1992, yesterday. The disarming of the employees and the disarming of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then it says: "On several occasions during the war ... police station, independently or with the Republika Srpska army, participated in combat operations ..." Apart from your participation in the operation at Renovica, did you take part in -- in any combat operations?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the month of August, upon an order by the chief, I went to the positions on Trebinic with an inspector of mine. We stayed there for four or five days. There were -- there was no fighting going on at the time. We just manned the positions in order to relieve the men who were normally there. And that's the only occasion when I went to the positions at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go in English, please, to the next page. And I believe -- yes, it's still on the same page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We see that 32 misdemeanour reports were submitted. And then the next paragraph: "At the request of the competent customs organs, assistance was provided 160 times mostly with moving certain persons in or out and seizing items owned by Muslim citizens." When it says "moving certain persons in or out," do you know to whom that refers?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then, finally, on this document, we need to go to the second page in B/C/S; it's bottom of the first page in -- second page in English. Do we see that -- just a moment. Let me see if I can find the actual paragraph. Yes. It's about halfway down the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do we see that: "Five interviews of police employees were conducted about the mistakes made in the course of their work. No disciplinary measures were pronounced against police employees." Now, we looked at the long list of -- of complaints that you made in your -- in your note. Whose responsibility was it to deal with -- or initiate disciplinary proceedings at the Pale SJB?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initiative for disciplinary procedures can come from anybody. However, when it comes to actually launching a disciplinary procedure, it is the head or the chief of the public security station who decides on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the event that the head of the public security station does not take disciplinary measures that he should, was the chief of the CSB, under which Pale came - in this case, Mr. Cvijetic - was he able to initiate disciplinary proceedings, if he received reports of misbehaviour by officers at Pale?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in a position to do that, I'm sure. And he could also send his officials to establish on the spot whether there are justified reasons to do so. I'm sure he -- he and they would have gotten involved in dealing with the problem. On one occasion, around this time, there were several complaints about the work of the various services in the station; not only mine, which were in a written form, but there were other complaints as well, from other people. A commission was set up; I don't know whether it was the minister who set it up or whether it was set up on behalf of the centre, but, in any case, it could not have been done without the consent of the minister of the interior. All sorts of illegal doings were noticed by the members of the commission, the officials who were also employees of the security services centre where Mr. Cvijetic was chief. And I believe that representatives of the MUP were also members of that commission. But I don't know what the consequences those men who had been involved in transgressions or disciplinary violations were -- suffered. The only woman who was a Croat who was still there before that, she lost her job at the time. That's what I remember. I know that. As she was an employee who worked in issuing ID, personal IDs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you said "about this time." Do you mean in 1993 or still in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that was in early 1993. Or thereabouts. Most probably that inspection or that control that was carried out was the result of the personnel shakeup when Pekic Petko took over from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't hear the first name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Took over from -- yes, took over from Malko Koroman, I think you said. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At the time when this commission was set up, was Mico Stanisic still the minister of the interior? Or was it in the period between his first appointment and his second appointment in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Korner. I believe it -- it has been established that the second appointment was not in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... if so, I've missed that. My understanding was he was reappointed at the end of 1993. If I've missed a piece of evidence, then, I'm sorry. But that's my understanding. If Mr. Zecevic can tell me on what that's based.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we have -- we had a number of -- we had a number of witnesses who confirmed the second appointment was in early 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, all right. I -- can I just leave it at that. I -- I withdraw the comment that I made, second appointment in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At the time of this commission, sir, was Mico Stanisic still the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember. I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That's all I want to ask about that report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1457, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just to deal, please, with this Malko Koroman, the takeover from Malko Koroman. Could you just look, please, for a moment at the document which is at tab 49, which is 1 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not on our 65 ter, and I'm not asking to exhibit it. But I just want the witness to deal with this. 103 -- 10373.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware that on the 11th of January of 1993 that - that's the reason for the handover that we saw - Mr. Koroman was assigned by Mr. Njegus, the assistant minister, to the Administration for Legal and Administrative Affairs of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. This is the first time I see it. I didn't know that he was assigned there. As far as I knew at the time, he was supposed to be assigned to a police station in Novo Sarajevo, Grbavica, Lukavica where the Security Services Centre was. He was supposed to be sent somewhere down there. And I know that he was very disappointed. As far as I know, he actually never left once he was removed from his position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. To your knowledge, now, were any proceedings, either criminal or disciplinary, taken against Malko Koroman as a result of the many complaints that you put in?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the time. After the war, however, yes. He was subject to certain proceedings; reports were filed against him. But I don't know whether anything came out of all that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now I want to, please, for a moment -- I'm going to come back to the complaints that you made at the end, but I want to deal with a couple of other issues, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Actually, before I leave it, can we just -- could we have up for the moment, document at tab 52, which is 2716. And could we have it not shown on the screen, please, for the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we can see at the head -- oh, it's a terribly bad copy in -- in the Serbian language. But is that a report again compiled by you in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime in May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yep. In it, you repeat a lot of complaints from 1992 and a sufficient number from 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, although it is actually on our 65 ter list, it does seem to me that it doesn't add anything. I'm merely adducing the fact that he went on complaining. And, indeed, I accept that in May 1993, of course, Mico Stanisic was not the minister of the interior. So it contains a repetition of the complaints from 1992 and new ones in 1993. But unless somebody else wants it in, I'm not proposing to exhibit it. I'm following Your Honours' directive not put in unnecessary documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can I turn, please, to a couple of other matters, general matters. First of all, paramilitary organisations that arrived at various stages in Pale. Were you aware of Arkan's Men arriving and, at some stage, staying in Pale?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard that name being used for them at the time, and I haven't heard of the presence of such persons, except on the occasion of an on-site investigation when we established that there was a group and that a member of that group had been killed nearby the Panorama Hotel. And we found out that he was a member of either the White Eagles or the Serb National Guard. I'm not sure. But there are minutes -- or, rather, there is a report, and it say there to which unit he belonged.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Was there also somebody called Gavrilovic and his group who were operating in Pale, Brane or Brne Gavrilovic.

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of Brne Gavrilovic. That was his name. I heard of that man but never saw him. I don't know whether or not he was in Pale, although he was born nearby. And I know that at the time he was in or around Ilidza with that group of his. Once, I believe that I was the duty officer at the station, then, a man from a nearby residential building came by and complained that two hours before he came to the station, some "Chetniks" had come to call on his wife. Those were the formations or the units that belonged to Brne. And they told his wife that she had to vacate the apartment by 6.00 p.m. And they had been around at around 4.00 p.m. That man was a Croat, he was employed by the VRS, and his wife is a Serbian woman. He told us approximately where they had gone, and I sent the police out to take a look around town. In the meantime, complaints had come in from some Muslims. And the three men, I believe that there were three, were caught in the old town of Pale, which is inhabited by Muslims. I understood that they had gone there to take their gold, et cetera. And the late Mr. Koljevic went there to calm down the situation. However, the police brought in these three men. They were drunk. And I placed them in custody where they remained for the night. And on the following day, Chief Koroman or one of the chiefs released them. On that occasion, they stated that they were from somewhere around Rogatica and that they were going to Ilidza and in that van which was seized there was some live lambs. They were very impertinent. They even threatened me because I had put them in custody. And that's what I know about these paramilitaries in Pale. Never again did I see anyone nor did I hear of anyone coming or passing through.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sir, thank you. At what party did you under -- or what organisation did you understand that this man Gavrilovic belonged to?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He belonged to the Serbian Radical Party; I'm certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who was the head of the Serbian Radical Party at that time?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I guess Seselj was the number-one man. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we look, please, at a couple of documents about the Muslims leaving.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we look, first, at 24 -- 65 ter 24 ... oh, sorry, I just want to check over my notes, if it's accurate. Yes, 2470.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, we looked yesterday at the -- the Assembly meeting where these decisions arose from. And this is Mr. Koroman reporting to the minister of the interior, 6th of July, about what has happened. And on the 30th of June, 88 Muslim citizens transferred. And on the 1st of July, 220 citizens transferred. Then 324. And on the 3rd of July, 410. Totalling just over a thousand people. Were aware of these transports, taking the Muslims out of Pale?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just before the -- the witness answers, Ms. Korner, you said: "And this is Mr. Koroman reporting to the minister of the interior."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I wonder based on what did you pose that question?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. I read it, because it says minister of the interior, but, of course, it's Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. It doesn't say to whom he is reporting, Mr. -- sir. Can you -- you tell us to whom such a report would have gone?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Who would -- on -- to whom would Mr. Koroman, as chief of the police station in Pale, be reporting about the -- the change of, as it calls, the place of residence of Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, given the hierarchy, he was duty-bound to submit that report to his immediate supervisor who -- and that was the chief of the CSB. But this may have been submitted to the president of the party. I can't know who he may have sent this to and whether he sent it out at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you say "the president of the party," which president -- which party?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the SDS party. I suppose that Mr. Koroman was an SDS member.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the question I asked was -- sorry, were I aware of effectively the, all together, a total of 4, 9, 16 buses, over a period of a few days, removing over a thousand people from Pale?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that they were leaving, but I didn't know on how many buses nor did I know how many of them had actually left.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this document please be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1458, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to -- could we have up on the screen, please, the document which is 2472. I'll just check that. Yep.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a document from the -- it looks like the Executive Committee of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, can we have a tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, it's 31.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I don't imagine that you've ever seen it before. Had you seen this document before until you looked at it --

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I want to ask you about something that's contained in it. It's complaining personally to Mrs. Plavsic about the fact that -- it says that Muslims are moving out forcefully and wilfully at their own private initiative. And then the criminal -- the illegal and criminal actions that have resulted, and so on and so forth. And it goes on to say this: "We believe that the provisions of the law governing the competences of police stations, which are linked vertically ... to the Ministry of the Interior do not involve coordination between them and the Assembly Executive Committees, which has resulted in the above-listed problems." And the -- in effect, they're proposing that you first collect information, opinions, from chairmen of other Executive Committees and try to solve the issue of responsibility of police stations, not directly to the Ministry of Interior but to the Executive Committees of the respective municipalities." Now, first, sir -- I should read the last paragraph: "We believe that forging the link ... could effectively prevent the incidence of crimes and other -- eradicate other current problems. "And we also find that no government, including a municipal one, can be effective if it is not supported by an organ or institution of enforcement. That will ensure the implementation of its decisions and conclusions." Sir, were you aware of tensions or complaints of the lack of cooperation with the Executive Committee of the Municipal Assembly and Pale SJB?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's asserted there that the police stations are linked vertically directly to the Ministry of Interior and therefore there was no obligation - that seems to be in the complaint - for them to either report to or cooperate with the Executive Committees. Was that your understanding of how the -- the Law on Internal Affairs worked?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I can see here that they're pointing out that the issue of responsibility in the work of the police stations must be resolved and that this is their suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this document please be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I understand the witness's testimony that he has commented on it. But he had never seen it before. He certainly wasn't the maker. What's the -- how does this come in through him?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the actions, Your Honour, that he can comment on. That's his right, that there was a vertical chain of responsibility. Your Honours, I accept that it's a tenuous link, but, realistically, there isn't anybody else. There's no other witness. We can apply to put it in through bar table, but there's no other witness that we're calling that can deal with this. So it's as simple as that. If the say that the link is too tenuous, I say we'll just have to apply to put it in through a bar table motion. But we don't have anybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, you were about to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you have already commented on one aspect of my objection. And only upon the subsequent explanation given by Ms. Korner we are convinced that there are not sufficient grounds for this document to be tendered through this witness. We believe that there are no conditions for that to happen. And as for the system of the functioning of the MUP and their relations with their local bodies, there is much evidence such as regulations. I believe that enough evidence has been tendered already. This is a rather shaky piece of evidence, whereas, we have much firmer evidence about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I needn't hear you in reply, Ms. Korner. I appreciate the -- taking on board Mr. Cvijetic's last observation about the -- this, as an item of evidence, being not as strong as other pieces of evidence that have been led. I nevertheless appreciate the importance of this for the case the Prosecution is trying to build. And whereas, perhaps, I shouldn't be persuaded by the argument that there's no other witness to -- through whom it can go in, having regard to the -- the context, and the witness has given evidence, it's admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1459, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, that's all that I think I want to ask you about moving out. And -- I'm sorry, there's -- I forgot to ask you -- paramilitaries, which is my fault because I can't read my own notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have a look, please, at document 37, I think it is. Just a moment. No, sorry. No, no, no, no. Yes, my fault. Could we look, please, at document -- the next document, which is 32. Oh, sorry. It's already an exhibit, but I want to ask about the signature. P317.17.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a certificate that has been issued by Pale SJB. Can you -- had you a chance to look at -- it's not really that clear on the screen, but you had a chance to look at it before. Can you tell us who signed that?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen this receipt before. This certainly is not the signature of the chief of the police station. Somebody signed in his stead. I can see it says "za," "for." And the first letter is J. It could only have been Jovicic. But if the last letter is the Cyrillic Ch, there still is no Cyrillic letter V. So it's difficult to say whether or not he signed it. But given the fact that the first letter is a J and the last letter is a Ch, it could be Jovicic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what -- and what position did he hold in the police station? I think we saw his name yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that, at the time, he was assistant commander. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if we looked at yesterday's document at the list of people at the station, he appears to be a sector leader. But by this stage he had been promoted to an assistant commander, had he?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sector leader ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us -- you mentioned yesterday the Yellow Wasps who were operating in Zvornik. Were you aware that Mr. Vojo Vuckovic was a member of the Yellow Wasps?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On what authority would Mr. Jovicic, if that is his signature, have been able to hand out this kind of weaponry to this person?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how anybody could have signed this instead of Malko Koroman, the chief. Possibly only Jovan Skobo. But given the fact that this is about such a person, I doubt that even he would have dared, or would -- would have been allowed to sign this. But without the approval of the chief, I doubt that this could have been handed out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what view do you take about the police, the authorised officials, handing out weaponry to members of a group that was neither military, official military, nor members of the police, a member of the police force?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's totally unacceptable and illegal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. That's all I want to ask you about that document. Now, finally, can I ask you to look at a group of -- some further documents that really arise out of the report that you wrote.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, next, at the document which is 2412, 32A.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a decision of the Executive Committee of the municipality on the 14th of July, where they're recognising the matters that you described yesterday, that the leaving - to put it neutrally - of the non-Serb citizenry, that there had been problems in listing their property which resulted in theft and unlawful use of abandoned property. And they have decided to create a revision committee. And on behalf of the Pale Police Station, crime inspector Goran Mumovic is to go on to this revision committee.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just redact that before it goes out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know that he had gone on to the commission?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he, in fact, join any commission, as far as you were aware, to do with -- dealing with the -- the property of non-Serb citizens?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember now, he did go to the municipality because the chief had tasked him with something. But I don't remember whether it was about this list of property or something else. He didn't inform me, and we didn't do anything particular about this either. Yes, we did do what we were able to do but not specifically about protecting this property, because the crime investigation service was small.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can that be marked and admitted -- admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1460, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you look now, please, at the document which has already been admitted as a Defence exhibit, I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 1D00183. And can we go to the -- yep, the second page, please, in each, English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is an order from the ministry itself. It looks like the - I hope I'm right in saying this time - the crime prevention administration, dated the 6th of August. And it's addressed, among other police stations, to yours. And it's all about the theft of these Golfs from the factory Tas. All I want to know, sir, is, we see many complaints about illegal possession of vehicles by members of the SJB; did you, as a police station, conduct any investigations into these Tas thefts?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid that answer will also have to be redacted before it goes out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that the only time that Mr. Macar from the crime prevention administration turned up at -- at Pale Police Station?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. That was not an only occasion. He turned up on -- turned up on several occasions on different matters. But he didn't come to me. He didn't come to inspect my work. He paid visits to the chief to discuss issues. But in that particular case he came to deal with that particular crime, and we had a discussion in my office on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As far as you understood, was a great deal of the MUP manpower - we see that it was addressed to a number of police stations, this document - spent on investigating these thefts? Or from -- the thefts from the Tas factory?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many people were involved. In any case, all the adjacent stations or stations around Sarajevo and especially in that part around Vogosca. I can't prove what I'm saying here, but I can say that a lot of officials were involved in all that. They stole vehicles, and they sold them on. Mr. Jovan Skobo also sold a vehicle to an Albanian in Kosovo during the war, and he issued him with the paperwork from the public security station, pretending that everything was legal. Later on, the vehicle was seized. There were checks. And when I went there and when I established that vehicle was not appropriately registered, however -- I mean, it did have a registration number, but under that registration number there is the name of a totally different owner. After my check which I carried out on the request of the MUP and after I reported back to the MUP, I heard - he didn't say that to me personally - I heard that Chief Malko Koroman paid a visit to that administration. And he was very angry, and he forbade him to ever go there. The officials told me that. I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next, could we have up on the screen, please, document 2704 but please not to go out to the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is an Official Note that is signed by you, and it's to do with this Teletina incident, which we looked at in your full report. For who -- for what purposes -- all I want to know is: Did you draft this Official Note? To who was it going to go.

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This Official Note was sent to the Security Services Centre, and I believe that I also sent it to the basic court in Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that, then, please be admitted and marked, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked, under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1641, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then could we have up, please, up next a document, 3369; but, again, not to go out to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, Ms. Registrar, I have a problem with my computer. I don't have LiveNote. It says "out of memory" or whatever. So if you can please help me with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand Mr. Zecevic is happy for me to carry on while they try and sort it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, this is, again, a document drafted by you, dated the 20th of December. And this time it's addressed to Mr. Cvijetic at the Security Services Centre. And it starts off by saying: "Because I opposed many incriminating activities of the leadership and other officers ... you have not taken any action, although you were informed about it promptly, that the leadership will probably become emboldened." And then you say that you were told that you weren't allowed to carry -- effectively carry out your duties by Chief Koroman. And then you were actually physically -- or threatened by Mr. Skobo at a meeting on the 16th of December. Did -- was what you put in that note truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1462, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, sir, let's come to the dealings you had with Mico Stanisic as minister. You've explained and we've looked at documents about the many complaints that you made about what was happening to Mr. Cvijetic. Did there come a time when you actually spoke directly to Mico Stanisic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of that year, I met Mr. Stanisic. Actually, I didn't meet him -- there was a meeting on Mount Jahorina, and I took the opportunity to talk to him for a couple of minutes and told him briefly that I had problems. And on that occasion, I asked him to possibly transfer me to the ministry, to assign me to the position of the inspector for traffic safety, which is what I did before the war. We didn't talk for too long. He was in a hurry. But did he promise me that he would do it, that I should come to the Bijeljina MUP in order to see things through. I went there on one occasion, actually at the first opportunity I went there; I saw him in passing. He was on his way to Belgrade at the moment. He told me to go to Milan Zuban [phoen], who was the chief of the police at the MUP at the time. He asked me to send an application to be transferred. I did that. I handed that application to Mr. Zubin, but the transfer never materialised. And I believe that it is more -- that it was more due -- down to Zuban, who was not a very conscientious person, not a very hard-working person who saw things through.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... so you saw him, is this right, first of all on Mount Jahorina, and then again in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us that you told him briefly that you had problems. When you say "problems," what problems were you telling Mr. Stanisic about?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember what exactly I told him. I don't think that I mentioned any specific cases. I just spoke in general terms about my problems with -- in working with the inspectors with Malko. I mentioned Mr. Skobo's threat. Malko was sitting there, and he didn't protect me. And then also I told him that I could not perform my job if I was forbidden from entering places and making checks, official checks, of the documents. And I wasn't left my choice. I had to go because there was no room for me there. I can't remember, but I'm almost sure that I did not mention any specific cases to him on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was your understanding of his knowledge of what was happening at Pale Police Station? What had been happening over the period from April to December; or November, when you saw him.

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? I assumed that he was aware of things, and let me tell you why. Chief Cvijetic was aware of many things. Mr. Cvijetic hails from Sokolac, and Mr. Stanisic hails from not far away from there. They knew each other. And in terms of the hierarchy and subordination, I believe that Zoran kept him posted, if not officially, then at least in his private capacity. He kept him posted about things they were -- that were going on. And I don't know that for sure; I only assumed that that was the case. Unless Mr. Stanisic had his own channels of information coming from Pale to him personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So sum that up, there were two reasons you made that assumption. The first was that there was the principle of the hierarchy and that Mr. Cvijetic was obliged to report to him, any problems; and, secondly, because they came from the same area, or roughly the same area?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, but I believe that is important. And, unfortunately, the last part of the answer of -- to the previous question was not recorded. I don't know if we need to go into the verification request or maybe the witness can -- can repeat. Because it wasn't recorded what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, sorry, we have occasional problems with interpretation. But you were -- you said you were telling me why you assumed he was aware of things. And you said: "... I believe that Zoran kept him posted, if not officially, then at least in his private capacity. He kept him posted about things they were -- that were going on ... I don't know --" I think that must be "for sure." Yes. I see that the transcript -- it's gone a bit haywire here. "... Mr. Stanisic had his own channels of information coming from Pale to him personally." Now, in particular, I don't know if that's what Mr. Zecevic is referring to, the sentence: "He kept him posted about things they were -- that were going on." And then we're not sure, and certainly what's recorded doesn't make sense. What did you say, sir? Can you just repeat it, if you can?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know what? It was only natural that the chief of the centre was supposed to inform the minister about the problems that he had in his areas where he was in command. And judging by that principle, I assumed that Mr. Stanisic knew, that he was aware, that he was on top of things. Both in terms of the official line and most probably in terms of their private line. The two of them hailed from the same area. They knew each other. It was also possible that Mr. Stanisic received all that -- that information, or maybe he checked the information that he had received, maybe he had a line of information that went straight to Pale, maybe he knew people who worked there. Because you never know who works for whom and what they do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you explained, however briefly, to Mr. Stanisic about the problems that were going on at -- at Pale station, did he ask you for any further information?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. You know what? He didn't ask for ... I talked to him as one human being to another. It was all in a rush. At that time, I had a place more -- most trust in Mr. Cvijetic and in Minister Stanisic at that time. I thought that they were the only ones that I could talk to. And if they couldn't solve my problem, then nobody else could. So, no, I -- I'm sure that we did not take the matter any further. It was a brief encounter, only in passing. Everything happened fast.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You weren't, as you told us, your request to transfer was not acted on. You remained at Pale Police Station. And as we saw, there was a change in the head. And as we also saw, however, there seemed -- there was still problems. So did you speak to Mico Stanisic again later on? And can I ask you straight away: Was he, at the time you spoke to him, on the third occasion, in fact, the minister again?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after the first encounter -- or, rather, after that encounter when we discussed my transfer and after that request was not met, I never requested a meeting with Mr. Stanisic. I believe that some changes occurred and that he was no longer minister. I don't think he was, actually. It was only at the beginning, and I originally thought it was at the end, however, it was at the beginning of 1994, most probably in February. On one occasion, Mr. Stanisic did come to Pale; and near the police station there are the offices of the ministry dealing with finances and accountancy. He paid them a visit. He has a room there. If he had to hold a meeting, that's where he would hold it. Or if he had other things to do, that's where he would do those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Your Honours, just a minor objection: We are leaving the frame of 1992. I don't know how relevant will the further line of questioning be. I don't want us to go much beyond the scope of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is relevant. If there's going to be a discuss about it, perhaps -- I see it's time for the break. It ought to be in the absence of the witness. And perhaps it can be -- we can have a couple of minutes before the witness come back in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We will take it up after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But I didn't -- of course, I'd hear what counsel has to say, but I thought the problem could have been addressed by Ms. Korner refining the question. But if counsel think that that is insufficient and there has to be some determination by -- by the Chamber as to the actual question, then we will do it in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the objection is coming because of the time-period. However, the nature of this particular meeting is relevant to various issues that have emerged in this case. Now, if Mr. Cvijetic still wants to argue it, then I'm perfectly prepared to. If Your Honours want advanced information about what this is about, Your Honours, it's at page 18 and 19 of the interview which has been uploaded into e-court. And we can also provide Your Honours with a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It only struck me, when I talked about refining the question, is that the answer of the witness was more -- was less precise than -- than the question, and the -- the answer that the witness provided probably formed the basis of Mr. Cvijetic's objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't -- I believe that Mr. Cvijetic's objection is because it's outside the period of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anyway, we'll take it up after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, my understanding - and I hope Mr. Cvijetic will confirm it - although he wants his objection to be noted, that I'm dealing with 1994, he doesn't want to argue it further. But perhaps Your Honours can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, unless he says anything to the contrary, we would proceed. So the witness can be escorted back to the stand. For my own purposes though, Ms. Korner, I would still prefer you to ask the question again with a view to seeking a more refined answer than the one the witness has given so far.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, in the sense that the witness has been off on a tangent, I'm leading into it, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, can I -- we were talking about the second -- sorry, third meeting you had with Mico Stanisic which was at the beginning of 1994. And you were explaining how it came about. Was this conversation with Mico Stanisic at Pale, and, again, was it about the problems that were still persisting in Pale?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now I'd like you to tell us --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I hope, Your Honours, that refines it more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was his attitude when he came to speak to you?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion, we had a somewhat longer conversation. There were just the two of us. I told him many things. I complained about my -- the residential status. I didn't have a place to live. There was a time when I slept in my office on a makeshift bed provided by my colleagues. I put him in the picture. I told him about the problems that were happening. The conversation was fair. We were honest to each other. He promised me that he would certainly solve all of the problems and that there would be personnel shake-ups very soon. That's what he told me "soon." And that was not the last conversation we were having. It was a somewhat longer conversation early in the afternoon, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then tell us now, then, about the last conversation.

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a few days later, five or six days, maybe not even five days, his driver called me up from Jahorina and told me that the minister had ordered me to wait for him in the room where we had met last. And I was there at the time. He came. He was extremely angry, furious, which surprised me greatly. I was flabbergasted. I entered the room where he usually holds meetings -- or held meetings when he was there. He told me to sit down, and I did. Then Mr. Stanisic - I don't know how to put it. It would be a bad thing for me to say that he shouted or hollered. But it was terrible for a highly educated man in such a high position, the way he behaved. And, thirdly, I felt like a slave. I didn't dare move. He walked up and down -- down the room, shouting, accusing me of obstructing this or that. I don't even remember what he was saying. And I didn't know what to -- could happen at any moment. And it went on for an hour at least. And I know that, once it was over, nobody could be found in the neighbouring offices. In that angry outbursts -- in those angry outbursts and in issuing threats to me, he went on, and I noticed that he was armed. He had a pistol in a holster. And he touched that holster several times. And I didn't know that -- what he might be able to do. I had never known him like that. I met him for the first time when I entered the service. And I knew the man, I thought -- and finally he said to me, extremely angrily, that on the following morning I would be out in the trenches with the military, somewhere on Mount Jahorina. And I said, No problem; I'll go to the trenches. But I'm sure that one day it will be known who did what, and that none of his accusations were founded. It went on for quite a while, and once he -- his anger subsided, I started talking, because I couldn't earlier. He wouldn't let me. And then I mentioned some specific cases that he had mentioned, that, let's say, investigator Milomir Gavrilovic had done that. And I asked him to have that man come and to see whether I was responsible or somebody else. And he, indeed, agreed. Milomir Gavrilovic was called to come, and he had a talk with him later. I wasn't present then. But before I finished my conversation -- actually, I left, and Gavrilovic arrived. I don't know whether it was on that day, because it was evening already, whether I met my chief. But I'm sure that I met him on the next morning. And I acquainted him with what had happened. And I told him that the cases that Stanisic had spoken about must be completed. It was about, among other things, the theft of a Golf vehicle that was the property of some dentist from Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you very much, sir. Just one other question about this meeting: You say that he uttered threats and one of them was that you would be out in the trenches the next day. Did he utter any other threats?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well -- well, there were no other threats. Only he reached for his pistol two or three times, and I wasn't armed. And given the state he was in then, I thought, He might as well kill me, possibly. Who knows? I had a hard time processing that, because I had known him for some 15 years before that incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, finally, sir - thank you - I just want to ask you about the record of the log-book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, before we leave this subject, I'd like to ask you, Mr. Witness, what the argument was really about at that occasion, between you and Mr. Stanisic. Because I'm not sure that I have fully understood what Mr. Stanisic's concerns were. He was accusing you, you said. But what did he accuse you of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that the reasons were the following: A Golf was stolen from that dentist. He was able to recover the vehicle by paying for it. I think that he paid 5.000 German marks. He had reported the theft of the vehicle, and Milomir Gavrilovic, the investigator, had received the report. And he was in contact with the -- the man about finding information about the perpetrators. It was in early December 1992. In mid-January, possibly around the 20th, I learned on the street from citizens by mere chance that the doctor had found his vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Witness, it is still not quite clear to me what the development was, because if I recall correctly, you started out by saying that you met with Mr. Stanisic a couple of times prior to the meeting in early 1994. And at the first occasion when you met him, you told him that you were unhappy with the way things were going in Pale, because your cooperation with your staff was not going well, and, as I understood it, there were crimes committed which were not - and deliberately not - investigated, and that was to your dissatisfaction. And so, if I understood you correctly, this was the subject of your concerns when you addressed Mr. Stanisic the first time. Now, what you have just told us now about your last meeting with Mr. Stanisic appears to me to be something completely different; namely, an issue about the theft of -- of a car from a dentist. And in -- I'm surprised that this could take Mr. Stanisic to such a level of rage that he would scold you for an hour about this. So was there anything else at the meeting in December -- in January 1994 which links back to your original complaints about the conditions in Pale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know what? That doctor wouldn't cooperate with us, even after his vehicle was returned. He didn't want to tell us who the perpetrators were. He said that they were MUP employees with stockings over their heads, that he knew some of them but he didn't dare say their names. And he went to Mr. Karadzic and told him about it. And I suppose that later on Mr. Karadzic called up Mr. Stanisic and that that was the reason. Apart from that vehicle, there was another vehicle which was a problem. I mean, there were more vehicles. But let me mention this one: It was a military vehicle which had gone off the road and landed in a ditch; and in a very short time, it was stolen. Although it was very heavy, so you needed actually a crane to pull it out of the ditch. I know that it was with the director of the radio television, Mr. Ilija Guzina, but he couldn't do anything about it. And that was also a problem. Maybe Mr. Karadzic demanded the minster that he do something about that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, did any of this have anything to do with investigation of crimes committed against non-Serbs in the Pale area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, finally, can I ask you to deal with the crime register from Pale Police Station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I explain. This is exactly like the documents that Mr. Olmsted was dealing with yesterday. It's a ledger. It's not been translated. There are certain statistics which have been extracted, which this witness - that's why we asked for the extra time yesterday - was able to confirm. And I'm just going to go through them. The Defence have them. I'm going to ask just that a page of the book be put up so that we can see what it's like. The book itself is 10388. And can we go, in it, to -- it should be - one, two, three, four, five - the sixth page, which bears the number at the top: 0700-7401.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And is that the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you will have to move it to the right-hand side so I can see the page number at the top. 0700 -- a bit more, please. Oh, all right. Well, can I -- I don't think it's the right page then because after the fourth entry there should be writing. The date -- the first date that one should see at the top of the page is 6/3/92. Now, I can't read a thing on the screen. But it doesn't look -- it's certainly not the right page, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want the one page. I'm sorry, there seems to be a -- seemed to have not told the Case Manager, which is our fault, that -- what page -- [indiscernible]. We're going to put the actual document. I just want identification of the writing. Oh, we're going to put it on the ELMO? How are we going to do that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, could the usher come and pick up the document, and we'll put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, this 10388 is not on your list of documents. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is. Yes. It was on the revised list. It's the last document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's not -- it's not on our 65 ter, and we've never had them translated, so -- expect for headings, which isn't -- all right. Got it, yes. But I'm afraid my -- it's my copy, so I scrawled -- but I didn't think of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, the writing in the middle of the page, this log-book, there was clearly a gap between the end of the joint MUP and the beginning of the new MUP, the Serbian MUP. Whose writing is that in the middle of the page?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean where it says "concluded"?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It's after the entry -- we can see there's a break in the entries and then we start again at number 1 in the entries, and there's some writing in the middle of that page, that writing. Can you just read out what it says?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Concluded or closed with entry number 37." I wrote that because, until that time, there was no war and there was no division of the MUP. With new criminal reports, these new reports were dealt with by the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before I deal with the statistics - sorry - what was the system in Pale Police Station? When would entries be made in that book? At the time a report was written? Or immediately on opening -- starting an investigation?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This log-book of criminal reports would contain only such reports which were duly completed and forwarded to the prosecutor's office at Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Can I just, then, deal with these statistics that you were asked to check and went through. I think there were a total number - and, indeed, when one goes to the end of that year, one can see - there were a total number of 60 criminal reports, but there were 65 that dealt with a total of 65 different allegations of crime?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There are only three criminal reports that you were able to find - and, indeed, so was the other gentleman that looked at it - where the victims of the crime were said to be that of Muslim ethnicity, judging by the names. And that was numbers 8, 11, and 30 in the book, the charges being, respectively, aggravated theft and two cases of murder. And in each case, the perpetrators were said to be unknown. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And there were no cases where Muslims were said to be the victims recorded and where -- or, in fact, there were only three, and the perpetrators were unknown; so it's obvious. The remaining 60 reports have Serb perpetrators and Serbs as the alleged victims. Is -- is -- is that right -- no, not the remaining 60, the remainder of the reports, once you've taken off those three?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there were also murders of Serbs committed by unknown perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Yes. Sir, thank you very much. That's all that I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before Mr. Cvijetic begins, I would remind -- I would point out to the witness and remind counsel that inasmuch -- especially because you speak the same language, to allow a gap between question and answer for the purpose of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I start, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, you are reminded to switch off your microphone after your question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know. I only wanted to ask the witness to pause, among other reasons, for me to be able to switch off the microphone so that it doesn't pick up the witness's voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I must address you as Witness. We've already agreed on that. I will mostly proceed along the questions asked to you by Ms. Korner. So I'm going to ask you about your appointment. The decision on your appointment was shown to you yesterday. That's 65 ter 2719. And you explained that this decision was -- bears an earlier date, namely that the 1st of April is mentioned as the date, although the decision was actually issued later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... he said he didn't get till later. He didn't say it was issued later.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Clearly my questions go in that direction. The witness knows what I'm talking about. But I would like to clarify with the witness the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of April, you were not able to receive such a decision because the ministry existed only on paper, it only had a minister and nothing else, and no services that could have drafted such a decision. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- can I -- I'm sorry to interrupt Mr. Cvijetic, but it is something I want to raise now and not have to get up and do again. We've discovered that when we're trying to analyse the evidence it's very difficult to find out what exactly the witness is saying because we have - and we're as much to blame sometimes as Defence, can I say straight away - it's compound questions. There are more than one fact contained in each of the question. So, for example, in this last question: "On the 1st of April, you were not able to receive such a decision because the ministry existed only on paper, it only had a minister and nothing else, and no services that could have drafted such a decision. Correct?" That's at least three propositions in one single question. And I am going to ask - and we're going to try and do the same - that we stick to one fact per question asked. It just makes it much simpler to work out what the witness is either saying or agreeing with. So if I can just make that point now so that I don't have to keep getting up and saying that. But it has really become a problem, as we've discovered, when analysing the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So, in other words, we all have to discipline ourselves. Please proceed, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wouldn't suggest for one moment that Your Honours should -- should follow this. I'm simply saying for counsel. I wouldn't be so bold as to suggest that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to discipline myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Witness, then, on the 1st of April, as I've already said, the ministry practically existed only on paper and had only a minister. And that minister had nothing at his disposal in the ministry apart from himself. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that. Even later, when I dealt with issues of -- concerning my years of service. I was officially employed by the MUP of BiH until the 6th of April. I don't know that there was a minister appointed as early as the 1st of April. No idea about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'll explain to you the crux of my issue. You will agree with me, will you not, that such decisions were issued to employees of the ministry in their interest for them to be -- to have their years of service acknowledged, and that's why the decisions bore earlier dates; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Answering to Ms. Korner's question, you spoke about your appointment in the earlier MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And you even said, I believe, that on the same day, together with Mr. Koroman, you attended a reception with representatives of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina because you were appointed together with them. Do I remember that correctly?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you directly. I don't need to remind you of your answer. That was in 1991. Do remind me of the name of that official of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Wait a minute before you answer.

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I -- that was in March that I was transferred, but I really don't remember the name of the man. But he was a Muslim, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Malko Koroman was chief before the establishment of the MUP of the RS; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And now let me ask you about something that happened in Pale. I would like to see whether you remember the event. Do you remember a protest rally which was organised in Pale after the attempt to remove Mr. Malko Koroman from his position by Mr. Mico Stanisic, at the very beginning?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember some activity of that kind, but I don't know what it was all about. I know that Mr. Stanisic was involved. Yes, I do remember, vaguely, that things likes that did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you also remember how big that rally was, how big the turnout was in Pale?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting -- the rally was really huge, and that Jovicic and Skobo and other men and a few others went around and recruited people to join the rally. I myself did not participate in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: According to the -- the information that the Defence has, there were several thousand people, and they unanimously provided support to Mr. Malko Koroman and effectively prevented Minister Stanisic from removing him from his position. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't answer, please. Look, there are three propositions in that one question, please. Firstly, was the rally really huge, several thousand people; second, did they unanimously provide support to Mr. Koroman; third, did they effectively prevent Mr. Stanisic from removing him. Now if you split those three things up, then we'll know what he is answering.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Witness, is it true that several thousand people attended that protest rally?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that there had been a lot of people, and I saw a group myself on the way to the town centre. They were passing by the police station. And as they were passing by, there may have been about 500 people in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. And that was just that one group that you saw, and there were 500 people in that group? My next question is this. And, now, let me ask you this: What was the purpose of that rally? Was it a protest against the removal of Mr. Koroman and support to Mr. Koroman [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did he receive the support at the local level? Did he remain in the position, despite the attempt to remove him?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at that moment, he did stay in the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Witness, within the context of that same question, let me just ask you one more thing: In Pale municipality, there was a Crisis Staff, right, there -- you heard of its existence?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that there were Crisis Staffs everywhere, in all the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one intervention in the transcript. It's line 18. I believe the witness's answer was: "Yes, at that moment, he did stay in that --" [Microphone not activated] I said: "He did stay in that position." That is what I heard the witness say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me take you back to a document that was shown to you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P650 is its number. There we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me just jog your memory. You saw the document yesterday. This is a statement provided by a Muslim police officers -- officer about their removal from Pale and -- and -- and their transfer to Sokolac. You do remember the document, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go straight to the following page in the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: First of all, do you remember the document that was shown to you yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: On page 2, you can see where reference is made in the second paragraph from the bottom the decision of the Crisis Staff for all Muslim policemen to hand in their weapons and the uniforms and equipment issued to them. And further on it says that the chief of the public security station explained the reasons. And that was a reciprocal measure for what had happened at the Stari Grad Public Security in Sarajevo. My question is this: You owe an explanation to us from yesterday. What had happened in Sarajevo in the public security station there, which provoked such a counter-measure, as it were?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that at the beginning of the month much March, the Serb police officers in the Stari Grad Police Station in Stari -- in Sarajevo were no longer desirable, were no longer wanted in that police station. They went to a place called Hresa. In other words, there was a division. A division took place. They were no longer allowed to work there. They went to Hresa, a place called Hresa, which is close to Pale, and for a while they were active there. And then after some time they joined the officers at the Pale station.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Are we talking about two municipalities that border on each other, Stari Grad and Pale?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And as you have told us, both events took place in March of that year?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For a while, the police officers from Stari Grad performed their duties and tasks in the territory of that municipality, at the check-point, at the entrance into Sarajevo on the main road. They did not perform their duties in Pale; that's what I'm saying. They were still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Within the context of your statement about the Crisis Staff, you see that this was done pursuant to a decision of the Crisis Staff. My question is this; and it has to do with the local authorities, and I am referring to the Assembly, the Crisis Staff, and others: To what extent did they have the power, the Crisis Staff and municipal authorities, to what extent did they have the power to influence events in -- in their areas at -- at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that those decisions had to be handed down from the highest political level, and they had to be implemented. Having said that, there are two different -- or three different lines. There's civilian authority, military authorities, and police authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We see here that the police security station also had to implement the decisions of the local authorities, like, for example, the Crisis Staff or the Municipal Assembly if the decisions concerned the activities of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now I'm going to move to another question, a different question. You told us that you had been involved in defence preparations at one point in your career, and you said that Mr. Koroman worked at a bank, that -- but that he was also involved in similar tasks, in defence tasks. Now just one general question: How do you mean that? How do you know what he did, at the bank that he was involved in? Defence preparations and regulations with this regard?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it only later -- heard that he had graduated with a degree and that he was involved in those tasks. It may not be correct, but that's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My question concerned the application of regulations concerning All People's Defence and civilian protection. Do you know that all legal subjects in the former Yugoslavia had to be -- prepared for defence, that they had to have books of rules and things like that?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I myself had friends who were assigned to perform those jobs and duties in different companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now I'm going to show you another document also shown to you yesterday, which is minutes from the 14th Session of the Municipal Assembly of Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 65 ter 2459. I don't know whether it was given a new number yesterday. I apologise if it was. Can we immediately go to the end of the document.
