More precisely, to bullet point 2. I believe it's page 5 -- or actually, no, one page before that. Page 4 in the B/C/S version. At bullet point 2. And we will need the corresponding page in the English version. Could somebody assist me with that? Now we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you provided your comment upon the session in question. I'm going to draw your attention to the part where it says: "In order to water down the discussion ..." Do you see the passage that starts with those words?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: A Working Group was set up in order to deal with the problem of immigration of Croats and Muslims and so on. And so a forth Working Group was established and so on and so forth. My question is this: Yesterday in answering Ms. Korner's questions, you said that you were not aware of the document about how Muslim citizens could change their place of residence and that was to be done at the public security station. And now you can see that it does stem from a decision of the Assembly, because the Assembly did deal with the issue?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw this. I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going to ask you something from your profession. Keeping records about the change of residence is one of the jobs of police stations; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: However, here, at the -- local body of authority orders the public security station to deal with the issue of mass emigration or change of residency of members of just one ethnic group, but you say you were not aware of this decision, so we will not invite any more comments from you. Do you remember, since we're talking about emigration, that a special MUP unit of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991 and 1992 ill-treated Serbs in an action to seize weapons when the Kezunovic house in that area was set on fire. Do you remember that incident?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, a slightly different point. What is this -- what's the relevance of this other than tu quoque? What has, indeed, any of this got to do with -- with either this witness or anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I tried to answer -- ask the witness whether he knew anything, just to know whether he had any knowledge; and if he didn't, then I would have dropped the issue altogether.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It doesn't matter whether he has got any knowledge or not. What's the relevance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Move on, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm moving on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You answered questions with regard to keeping people confined in the cinema hall, and you said that you are not aware of any details, that you only have second-hand information that you learned subsequently. Since you worked at the police, I can ask you this: Keeping people in the cinema hall, could this have -- provide from the documents of the Crisis Staff and the Municipal Assembly, just like things were done pursuant to the other two documents that I have just shown you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Anything could have happened. This witness has dealt with his knowledge. Now, unless he knows, it's no good him answering this question either because it's pure guess-work.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this or not? Just tell us briefly, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You participated in the Renovica operation personally; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could you just briefly explain how the two policemen got killed? They were policemen, were they not? But just be brief, please.

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know how Goran [indiscernible] got killed. He was in the same vehicle where I was, and he was in the same group that was supposed to go with me to that village. As he was getting off the truck, shooting already started in Renovica, we were just a little before Renovica where we pulled -- when we pulled over. As we were getting off the truck, the first group got off and took the lower, the southern, path, and I got off and I jumped into a trench on the upper path, together with a few colleagues. As we were getting off the vehicle, there was shooting from all sides from the mountains that surrounded us. And at one point, at the place where Goran left on the southern side, there was a piece of tin, and you could hear the bullets, the sounds of bullets, on that piece of tin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I did not want all those details. I'm interested in an agreement about the voluntarily surrender of weapons, had that been reached, and how all that transpired. Was there an ambush; were you ambushed? That was the gist of my question.

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I was told, that there had been an agreement between Malko Koroman and Alija Prazina, the president of the SDA. But when we went up there, we were caught unawares; whereas, the Muslims were organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And it only remains for me to deal with your report. That's 65 ter 317. There are some details that haven't been commented upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we immediately turn to the following page of the report. I need the fifth paragraph from the top. So in the English version, we also need the fifth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in this part of the report, you speak about a problem that arose due to the migration or the departure or the change of residence of this or that part of the population which was a result of the war. You will agree with me, won't you, that this made the security situation on the ground more complex. And it also gave rise to an increase of inter-ethnic tension. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You even say here that in such a situation the staff the SJB couldn't do much to prevent that. Does that mean that you consider this to be force majeure, that you couldn't -- upon which had you no influence?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because all the other relevant services had failed, and the police itself couldn't do much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now go to, I believe, page 4 in e-court. And we'll need the third paragraph; could we please zoom in on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Here you speak about a situation that, I suppose, was a general problem. Namely, that you weren't able to reach the injured party, but, in spite of that, you drafted Official Notes and, thus, documented the perpetration of such an offence. Is that the meaning of this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honours. I don't know which paragraph -- he says paragraph 4 in the B/C/S, but I'm not sure that the English is reflecting that. Could we just ... Could you read out the beginning of the paragraph or tell us what page it is in English? No ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last paragraph of this page in the English translation; whereas, in the original, it's the third paragraph from the top. It starts with: "In addition to ..." this number of criminal reports submitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Witness, in this context, I just want to ask you: No matter whether the perpetrator was known or unknown, whether the injured party is there or not, it was your duty under the law to document such a criminal offence. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is that what you did?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could unused microphones be switched off.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: With regard to the implementation of the regulations, did you also receive instructions from the headquarters of the ministry to proceed that way. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether we were receiving any at the time. But that was the procedure, so I don't remember whether we had special instructions to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, then, that the first authority in your work was the law, so you didn't have to ask many questions in doing about your -- in going about your job; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Then the law doesn't distinguish between perpetrators based on ethnicity, and the same applies to injured parties or victims. So that means that you had to treat all these the same way; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that's how I treated them too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because in this report of yours, pointing out the problems that you faced in the work of the police station, you efficiently observed laziness and irresponsibility, even when the victims are Serbs and the cases were not duly processed. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This duty of yours included the uncovering and documenting of even the most serious criminal offences, such as war crimes. I mean in the sense that you didn't distinguish, depending on who the perpetrator and the victim was, and it was your duty to process all this the same way. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'll show you a document, because I believe you mention it in your statement, and that's the RZ form.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see document 1D63.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... tab number, please, in your documents. Oh, I've got it. That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do look at this accompanying letter, before I show you the form, and the introductory part states what I have just said; in paragraph 2: That this is done in equal manner, irrespective of the ethnicity, being a Muslim, Croat. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page so we can see the form.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have to go further back. Yes, this is the form.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Take a look at entries -- or lines 5 and 6. They read "ethnicity and religion." This is blank, and it is expected that these data be filled in on the spot, and that no distinction is made, depending on the ethnicity of the person in question? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Witness, in your work, you said, I believe, that this is exactly how you proceeded; correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Finally, sir, let me remind you something you said. You said that you had -- trusted your chief, Zoran Cvijetic, fully, and also the minister, Mr. Stanisic. What does that stem from?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know Mr. Cvijetic before, but after the initial contact, and subsequently -- well, I don't know. The man always was willing to see me and hear what I had to say. And, well, I'm not saying that it was all up to him but possibly to his subordinates who were my superiors. I also knew Mr. Stanisic before. I knew him very well. And we were on good terms when he worked at the city SUP and then went to the economy and then came back to the city SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you trust him now?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to put it. Do I or don't I trust him? I am really offended by [as interpreted] a human being because of what happened to me. I don't hate him because I don't hate people, generally speaking. But now, well, my attitude has changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to ask you something else. Do you know about the meeting of the executives in the crime investigation area from the CSB of Romanija-Biska [phoen], which was attended by the SJB Pale representative? I'll show you the report to jog your memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not mention the witness. This document is about a meeting that dealt with problems at Pale. But since it's time for the break now, I can accept your suggestion that we should go into private session and -- in order to protect the witness's identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. When we return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Before the break, I called up a document. Could it be returned. 65 ter 1273.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In the middle of that document or in the middle of page one, Mr. Tusevljak points to certain objective difficulties in the work of the crime services of all centres, not only in Pale. There's a lack of technical equipment, there's no communication between the SJB and the CSB, lack of personnel in numerous SJBs, and so on and so forth. You can see it for yourself, if you look at the screen. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you have some, if not all, of the problems in your work in Pale?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, your answer was not recorded. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had the same problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to the following page in the B/C/S version. I'm interested in the last paragraph. In the English version, it will probably be page 3. Nikolic Radomir was the next speaker. In the English version, I believe we have to go to the following page; the one after this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: On both pages there - it is the last paragraph - your colleague from Ilidza points to the problem of the report of the damaged party in cases, they experience a burglary or a theft, and the service having problems with finalising a criminal report. Did you have similar problems?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In my question, there's something lacking. "When it comes to injured parties who are Muslims." Can this be added? And when you said "Yes," you had in mind the same situation, when the injured parties were Muslims and there were no reports or no documents, you had a problem in finalising your criminal report and forwarding it to the prosecutor. Wasn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And now I don't want to dwell upon this document because all of your colleagues pointed out their own problems, but I would like to move on to the last page with the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move to the last page in the document, please. In B/C/S version, it's page 5. Actually, on the last page with the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the conclusions, and we will probably provide just a brief comment upon all -- upon them. Did you read the conclusions, please? From what you have told us already, it seems that you pointed to the most part of the conclusions in your written documents and letters about the problems in your work. Am I right.

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I still need to ask you this: Did you have any problems in communicating with the centre? Because a reference is made here to the lack of communications and lack of telephone lines and things like that. Did you experience the same problem in Pale?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And, finally, as can you see under 6: "Maximal engagement of all the operational workers is required for the tasks of documenting war crimes, and the injured parties and perpetrators are not segregated in terms of their ethnicity." Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since this document has not been admitted and there are no objections, I would like to tender the report -- or, rather, the minutes of the meetings of officials in charge of the line of the witness's work be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before we take a position on that, Mr. Cvijetic, could we inquire from the witness the information contained in point 2 of the conclusions. Because my question is, to the witness, whether this was actually functioning in practice. In other words, were the CSB and the SJBs able to bring information back and forth on every Saturday, as it is proposed in the conclusion? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that I took our official car to attend meetings on Saturdays, meetings where we discussed such problems. And on other days as well, whenever a need arose, because there was hardly any other way to communicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, Mr. Witness, at least once a week, on Saturdays, you were able to exchange information between the CSB and the SJB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember whether that happened every Saturday, but it was frequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And do you recall how many SJBs were present in those meetings with the CSB? Just roughly, if you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some couldn't attend. It all depended on the conditions on the roads. It was not easy to get from Ilidza, sometimes even impossible. But most of us were there. We always had a majority present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can you name some of the SJBs who were normally present in those meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] People came from Sokolac. I came from Pale. People came from Han Pijesak as well. Ilidza and Rajlovac attended as well but not regularly because of the problems on the road, but they did come. I'm not sure about Zvornik; I don't know whether they attended. Zvornik, Milici, Sekovici, Skelani, Vlasenica; I'm not sure whether anybody came. Because I know that there were meetings in those areas with their respective heads of crime prevention and detection services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will become Exhibit 1D328, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And finally, I believe that Ms. Korner drew our attention to the fact that we did not provide precise explanation as to the pensionable years and how they were combined. I'll try to put a very precise question to you, and let's help the Trial Chamber understand what happened. When the employees of the former MUP of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina who were of Serb ethnicity moved to Pale, most of them did not join that service on the 1st of April. They joined later. However, in their decisions on appointment, the 1st of April is indicated as the day when they started working in the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska. I have just put things to you, and let me say that this was done in order for them to have the pensionable years in the former MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the pensionable years in their next job, to avoid a 15-day gap which would have reduced their pension prospects. Was my explanation good?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that that was kept in mind. I know that, for myself, that the period from the 1st to 6th was not recognised as pensionable years because I was still on the record in Sarajevo where I remained working until the 6th of April. From the 6th of April, I started working in the MUP of Republika Srpska; that's when I formally joined.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that that was in the interests of all of us, of all of you MUP members that might have suffered from the temporal gap in the pensionable years?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't confirm that. For me, the war started on the weekend of the 5th. And as of the 6th, I could no longer go back to my apartment. So I don't know whether the MUP of Republika Srpska started working on the 1st. I don't know. I -- I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In your case, there could not have been overlapping, in terms of those six days. Those six days could be recognised only in one place: Either in the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the MUP of Republika Srpska. So there was no way that that period could have been duplicated, so things were done properly in your case?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is the position of the Zupljanin Defence as was previously indicated, that they don't intend to cross-examine this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we don't have questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've just got one question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, where exactly was the CSB Sarajevo for the Serbian Republic based?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was based in Lukavica, in -- in a factory; the factory was Energoinvest. That was in one part of Sarajevo which was under the Serb control.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And roughly how far was that from Pale?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly, perhaps, 20 kilometres. But it was not easy to get from one place to the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In Pale, however, as far as communications were concerned, if necessary, did you have access to the government communications?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't know that. I had no contacts with the government, so I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, have someone at Pale SJB whose job it was to deal with communications?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were two police officers there. We saw them on one of those lists that you showed me. And their job was encryption. But those were special communications. They were in charge of communications. But, as I said, those were special lines of communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And, finally, in respect of your reports to the CSB, in particular, the ones we looked at which contained the complaints, how were they sent? Did you deliver them personally, or were they sent via the dispatch system?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we saw was delivered by me personally. If it had gone along the lines of hierarchy, Chief Koroman would have had to see it. But, in that case, it wouldn't have been dispatched. So I gave it to Chief Cvijetic on the occasion of those meetings that we mentioned a short while ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, sir. I've got no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could I put to you just one follow-up question in relation to the meetings that we talked about just a while ago between the CSB and the SJBs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: First of all, did the meetings take place in Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some meetings were held in Lukavica, for those who were near and able to come. But I remember meetings at Han Pijesak, for that region. And where I was, at Pale, I was -- I went to a meeting to Milici. That was also far away. But the rest of them were at Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And at those meetings, were the MUP also represented, or was it just the CSB who, sort of, chaired the meetings?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, does Your Honour mean MUP headquarters -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Oh, so sorry. Yes. Yes, from the ministry, MUP headquarters.

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I remember, somebody was always present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you remember who?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember Investigator Ratko Kapetanovic. Goran Macar was also there; he was the chief of the crime investigation service. I don't remember any others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Was it your impression that the representative from the minister would report back to the ministry and bring back the information that he had picked up at the meetings?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was supposed to function; that was the logic. The minister, through his services, along the lines of work, was supposed to be informed of all problems. Whether that was, indeed, the case, whether that really functioned that way, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And did the representative from the ministry offer information to the participants in the meetings with the CSB and the SJBs?

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall now to what extent they participated. But I know that all of us discussed some problems. Of course, some of us had more problems; some -- others had fewer, depending from where they were. However, it was -- although it was good to talk, the problem was that the situation on the ground didn't really change. Why, whether for objective or subjective reasons, is another matter. I could not have films developed because there was no lab. I had to ask a private photographer to come to a room and do that for me. It was a -- a private request from me to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I see. My question was merely to -- to discover if the representative from the ministry was able to provide instructions or information from the ministry to the participants in those meetings so as to ensure that whatever decisions were made at the central level in the ministry would be communicated down to the CSBs, and, from there, to the SJBs. So that's why I asked you if the representative did take the floor and -- and provide you with information from central headquarters.

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did take the floor. And that's how we got some information. But, otherwise, it was communicated to the chief of any station, and the station would inform us, depending on the line of service we were in, about what we were supposed to do and how we were to -- supposed to behave. For example, the movable property: That was a matter that was with a government decree, outlining what was to be done and how; so there couldn't be any anarchy in which anybody could do what they deemed right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That's all I have to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, again, an intervention in the transcript: 66/5. On Your Honours' question, the witness was mentioning something about the instructions, and that wasn't recorded. I don't know if that was translated at all. Maybe ... maybe can he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you please repeat the last part of your answer to me.

utterances.speaker: ST-127 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had some instructions in the form of documents received from the Ministry about how we should work. It was all in accordance with the law. These documents only explained how certain matters were to be dealt with most easily. And also, it was also about the implementation of other rules and regulations as well as decrees. There was this very important decree, namely, the government decree about the treatment of the spoils of war; and that was mostly about immovable property that was left in the area, abandoned and what have you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We thank you, sir, for your assistance to the Tribunal. And you are now released as a witness. And we wish you have a safe journey back to your home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't know if there are any housekeeping matters that need delay us, because, if so, the usher can wait until we rise to escort the witness from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. No, there aren't, Your Honours. Except that - it's the same situation - the estimates for the Defence are -- are slightly excessive at the moment, and we haven't got a witness here for tomorrow because the estimate was four hours, I believe, from Stanisic, and there was also something in for the Defence of Zupljanin. I know it's difficult. And we normally run over what we say. But I think, rather than having days off which haven't been organised, as it were, this is one that Your Honours will and we will have to have, it might be an idea if, after the Defence have given their original estimates, which we've asked for so we can start planning, if those estimates change, they could let us know so we can bring up more witnesses. Clearly, we're anxious to move this case on, as Your Honours are, as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may respond. Your Honours, we under fully the situation, but when we have a viva voce witness, the only indication for us is the length of direct examination because at that point we do not know which of the documents will the -- will -- will the Office of the Prosecutor use with the witness. So in order to be on the safe side, we have to give the estimates. Only when we hear the witness and the documents are presented to him can we only then say -- that is -- that is the first point in time when we can really give a roughly estimate which -- which we are going to actually keep. I hope you understand our position. I -- I'm sure Ms. Korner does. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- the -- whereas, I suppose, everybody is frustrated by these dies nons, if we look at the -- what has happened over the past several months, an occasion like today is really exceptional. So the Chamber is not yet alarmed by overestimates or -- or overbooking of time, as it were, by the Defence. But if it -- if, as we progress, it appears to be a problem, then we would invite counsel to look again at the way that they -- they do these things. So we take the adjournment, to reconvene in this courtroom on Monday -- Monday morning. And I trust everyone has a safe weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 21st day of June, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
